You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor-node load RL from a piezo transducer.
    *   Constraints:
        *   `vout_min`: $\text{vavg} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$
        *   `vout_max`: $\text{vmax} \le 3.6\text{ V}$
        *   `ripple`: $\text{vpp} \le 0.05\text{ V}$
        *   `startup`: $\text{tup} \le 0.4\text{ s}$
        *   `settled`: $\text{dv} \le 0.02\text{ V}$
    *   Piezo Model: Current source $I_p \sin(2\pi ft)$ in parallel with $C_p$ (25nF) and 20M$\Omega$ resistor.
    *   Operating Conditions: S1 (nominal), S2 (heavy load), S3 (strong excitation/light load), S4 (weak excitation), S5 (low freq), S6 (hot/high $C_p$).

    *   Design 1 ('SSHI_FBR_Zener'):
        *   Topology: L-S (SSHI inversion) $\rightarrow$ Full Bridge Rectifier (FBR) $\rightarrow$ Zener clamp $\rightarrow$ Storage Capacitor.
        *   Results: Fails on power (S2, S4, S5), startup (S1, S6), settling (all), and ripple (all).
        *   Screening: Passed (delivered plenty of power when $V_{\text{out}}$ was fixed at 1.8V).
        *   Problem: The L-S combination at the input is acting as an SSHI-like inverter, but it's integrated into an FBR. However, the FBR has 2 diode drops. The voltage $V_{\text{out}}$ is drifting and ripple is high, suggesting $C_{\text{out}}$ might be too small or too large, or the charging efficiency is low. But the "settled" failure (dv too high) and "startup" failure suggest the time constant $\tau = R_L C_{\text{out}}$ is too long or the power delivered is barely enough.
    *   Design 2 ('SSHI_Greinacher_Zener'):
        *   Topology: L-S $\rightarrow$ Greinacher (Voltage Doubler) $\rightarrow$ Zener $\rightarrow$ $C_{\text{out}}$.
        *   Results: Failed screening (delivered almost no power). This is likely because the Greinacher requires the input voltage to overcome diode drops in a specific sequence, and the L-S inversion might have messed up the timing or voltage levels.

    *   The FBR (Design 1) had poor performance because it's essentially a passive rectifier with a boost (L-S) at the front.
    *   The "S3: strong excitation, light load" passed everything, but $V_{\text{out}}$ reached 3.41V. Without the Zener, it would have exceeded 3.6V.
    *   The main issues are:
        1.  Power delivery at low excitation/heavy load (S2, S4, S5).
        2.  Slow startup and settling.
        3.  High ripple.
    *   *Self-Correction:* The FBR in Design 1 is a standard full bridge. If we use a synchronized switch harvesting on inductor (SSHI), we typically don't use a full bridge. We use a half-bridge or a specific arrangement of switches and diodes.
    *   The L-S part in Design 1 (`L1` from `pzp` to `n1`, `S1` from `n1` to `pzn`) is a basic SSHI flip. It inverts the charge on $C_p$.

    *   Standard SSHI often uses a bridge or a specific diode-switch network to move the inverted charge to the storage cap.
    *   Wait, the FBR in Design 1 was `D1[pzp, out], D2[pzn, out], D3[0, pzp], D4[0, pzn]`. This is a standard bridge.
    *   Combining L-S with FBR: The L-S part flips the voltage on $C_p$, but the FBR then takes the rectified version of that.
    *   The power delivered in the screen was high, but in the simulation, it failed. This often means the "startup" from 0V is the bottleneck. At $V_{\text{out}} = 0$, the diodes are forward-biased and the L-S circuit is working, but the energy transfer might be inefficient.

    *   A simpler, more efficient way to extract energy is the "Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction" (SECE) or a modified SSHI.
    *   Let's try a standard SSHI topology:
        *   Piezo terminals: `pzp`, `pzn`.
        *   Flip circuit: `L1` and `S1` (as in Design 1).
        *   Rectification: Instead of a full bridge, perhaps a simpler half-bridge or a Greinacher that actually works.
        *   Wait, look at the Reference Design (FBR). It failed S2, S4, S5. This means we *must* increase the voltage or the efficiency.
        *   The SSHI (L-S) increases the available voltage from the piezo.
        *   Let's try a "Standard SSHI" (not FBR):
            *   Flip: `L1(pzp, n1), S1(n1, pzn), G1(SYNC, edges=both)`.
            *   Extraction: `D1(pzp, out), D2(pzn, out), D3(0, pzp), D4(0, pzn)` (This is the FBR).
            *   Wait, that *is* what Design 1 was. Why did it fail power on S2, S4, S5 despite passing the screen?
            *   Screening fixes `Vout = 1.8V`. This removes the startup problem and the $V_{\text{out}}$ drift.
            *   The "settled" failure ($dv > 0.02\text{V}$) and "ripple" failure ($vpp > 0.05\text{V}$) strongly suggest the output capacitor $C_1$ is too small. But if $C_1$ is too large, "startup" ($t_{up}$) and "settled" ($dv$) fail.
            *   Wait, the Reference Design had $C_{\text{out}} = 2.2\text{ $\mu$F}$. Design 1 had $C_{\text{out}} = 10\text{ $\mu$F}$.
            *   If $C_{\text{out}}$ is $10\text{ $\mu$F}$ and $R_L$ is $150\text{ k$\Omega$}$ (S2), $\tau = 1.5\text{ s}$. This explains why $dv$ (the change between 0.6-0.7s and 0.7-0.8s) is high—it hasn't reached steady state yet!
            *   To fix "settled" and "startup", we need a *smaller* $C_{\text{out}}$, but to fix "ripple", we need a *larger* $C_{\text{out}}$. This is the classic tradeoff.
            *   *However*, if the power delivered is higher, the startup is faster and it settles quicker.

    *   Is there a more efficient way to move charge?
    *   What about a "Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor" (SSHI) where the inductor is used to flip $C_p$ AND the rectifier is more efficient?
    *   Let's try a "half-bridge" SSHI:
        *   Piezo: `pzp`, `pzn` (connected to 0).
        *   L-S Flip: `L1(pzp, n1), S1(n1, 0), G1(SYNC, edges=both)`.
        *   Extraction: `D1(pzp, out), D2(0, pzp)` (No, that's not right).
    *   Let's try a different approach: a Charge Pump (Dickson or similar) or a Boost converter. But we only have `S` and `SYNC`.
    *   Wait, the `SYNC` controller allows us to close the switch at the extrema.
    *   Let's try a "Parallel-SSHI" (PSSHI) or just a better tuned FBR-SSHI.
    *   Actually, let's look at the "Greinacher" again. Design 2 failed screening. Why?
        `D1(pzp, n2), C1(n2, 0), D2(n2, out), C2(out, 0)`.
        This is a voltage doubler. If `pzp` is the input, the charge from $C_p$ is pumped into $C_1$, then into $C_2$.
        The problem was the `L1-S1` flip. If `S1` flips the voltage on $C_p$, the Greinacher should still work.
        Wait, Design 2: `L1(pzp, n1), S1(n1, pzn)`. `pzn` is not ground! The piezo is `pzp` and `pzn`.
        If the Greinacher only uses `pzp` and `0`, but the piezo is `pzp` and `pzn`, we are missing half the energy.

    *   Piezo: `pzp`, `pzn`.
    *   Symmetry is key. Use an FBR but optimize the $C_{\text{out}}$ and the SSHI part.
    *   Wait, if Design 1 passed the screen (meaning it *can* deliver the power), but failed the simulation (startup, settling, ripple), the problem is almost certainly the value of $C_1$ and the time it takes to charge.
    *   To reduce ripple *without* increasing $C_1$ too much, we need the energy to be delivered more continuously. But the piezo is $100\text{ Hz}$.
    *   Maybe the Zener is clamping too early? No, $V_{\text{out}}$ was around $2\text{V}$.
    *   Let's try a different SSHI:
        Instead of `L-S` and `FBR`, let's use a "Synchronous Switch" to transfer charge from $C_p$ to $C_{\text{out}}$ directly.
        `S1(pzp, out)`, `S2(pzn, out)`. (Too simple, doesn't invert).
    *   Let's try a "Boosted" Rectifier:
        `L1(pzp, n1), S1(n1, 0), G1(SYNC, edges=pos, phase=0)`
        `D1(n1, out)`
        This is like a boost converter.

    *   Wait, I have a better idea. The "Reference Design" (FBR) failed $V_{\text{avg}}$ on S2 and S4.
    *   $V_{\text{avg}}$ on S2: $1.76\text{V}$ (needs $1.8\text{V}$).
    *   $V_{\text{avg}}$ on S4: $1.51\text{V}$ (needs $1.8\text{V}$).
    *   This means the FBR is *almost* enough. The SSHI inversion should provide more voltage.
    *   In Design 1, $V_{\text{avg}}$ on S2 was $1.76\text{V}$ (still!). And S4 was $1.21\text{V}$ (worse!).
    *   Why did the SSHI (L-S + FBR) perform worse or same as FBR?
        Because the L-S flip happens *before* the FBR. The L-S flip inverts the voltage on $C_p$, but if it's not timed perfectly or if the inductor value is wrong, it can actually waste energy or oppose the flow.
        In Design 1, `ton` was $49.7\text{ $\mu$s}$. For $L=10\text{mH}$ and $C_p=25\text{nF}$, $T_{\text{res}} = \pi \sqrt{LC_p} = \pi \sqrt{10^{-2} \cdot 25 \cdot 10^{-9}} = \pi \sqrt{2.5 \cdot 10^{-10}} \approx 3.14 \cdot 1.58 \cdot 10^{-5} \approx 49.6\text{ $\mu$s}$.
        The timing was correct. So why the poor performance?
        Ah! The L-S flip `L1(pzp, n1), S1(n1, pzn)` happens at the peaks. This inverts the voltage $V_{pzp} - V_{pzn}$. But the FBR also sees this.
        Actually, if you flip the voltage on $C_p$ using a switch across the piezo, you aren't necessarily increasing the *rectified* voltage unless you do it in a way that the rectifier can capture the flip.

    *   A better SSHI:
        The flip should happen, and then the charge should be moved to the storage cap.
        Standard SSHI topology:
        - Inductor $L$ and switch $S$ are in parallel with the piezo.
        - A rectifier (or just diodes) is used to move the charge.
        Wait, the "FBR" is a full bridge. If you put the L-S in parallel with the piezo, the FBR is still there.
        The problem might be the diode drops. A full bridge has 2 diode drops ($2 \times 0.25 = 0.5\text{V}$).
        If we use a "Half-Bridge" or "Greinacher", we might reduce the drop.

    *   Let's try a "Charge Pump" style approach using the `SYNC` switches.
        `S1(pzp, n1), G1(SYNC, edges=pos)`
        `C1(n1, 0)`
        `S2(n1, out), G2(SYNC, edges=pos, phase=0.1)`
        This is getting complex. Let's stick to simpler topologies.

    *   What if we use a "Synchronous Rectifier" instead of a diode bridge?
        `S1(pzp, out), G1(SYNC, edges=pos)`
        `S2(pzn, out), G2(SYNC, edges=neg)`
        This would have almost zero drop!
        But wait, this would just connect the piezo directly to the output. The output would be a sine wave. We need a storage capacitor $C_{\text{out}}$.
        If we use switches `S1, S2` and $C_{\text{out}}$, we need to make sure we don't discharge $C_{\text{out}}$ back into the piezo.
        So: `S1(pzp, out)` is not enough. We need a diode: `D1(pzp, out)` and `D2(pzn, out)`. But that's just a half-bridge.
        Wait, the FBR (Reference) failed because of the 2-diode drop and low energy.
        If we use a *Half-Bridge* (2 diodes), the drop is only $0.25\text{V}$.
